item.title: iQOO's Gaming Tablet Has a Built-In Fan. That's Not Even the Best Part.
item.description:
Gaming tablets have a size problem. Most manufacturers assume you want an 11- or 12-inch screen, as if portability doesn't matter once you've committed to a tablet. iQOO clearly disagrees. The iQOO Pad Ultra, launching in China on September 29, packs flagship-level gaming hardware into an 8.8-inch OLED display. It's the kind of spec sheet that makes you wonder why everyone else insists on turning tablets into portable monitors.

The Pad Ultra runs Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the just-announced chip that maxes out at 5GHz and should score over 4 million on AnTuTu. iQOO pairs it with up to 16GB of RAM, which showed up in a recent Geekbench listing. But here's where it gets interesting: iQOO built an active cooling fan directly into the tablet. You've seen this in a handful of gaming phones like the iQOO 15 Ultra, but it's rare in tablets. Combined with iQOO's custom Q4 gaming chip, the Pad Ultra promises 2K resolution gaming at 165fps with full-scene ray tracing and what the company calls "Q-flex control technology" to reduce input latency.

The 8.8-inch form factor makes this thing genuinely one-handed in a way that most gaming tablets aren't. The OLED panel should deliver at least 2K resolution and 120Hz refresh, though iQOO hasn't confirmed exact specs yet. There's a hole-punch front camera, slim bezels, and color options in Ender Black or Star Silver. The square camera module and visible cooling vent give it a distinct gaming-hardware look that won't be mistaken for an iPad.

iQOO stuffed a 9,000mAh battery inside, which is impressive given the compact footprint, and it charges at 66W. For context, that's faster than most tablets this size and should mean reasonably quick top-ups between gaming sessions. The tablet also includes built-in livestreaming tools with native high-frame-rate output and automated highlight clipping, so it's clearly aimed at people who want to broadcast their gameplay without juggling extra apps.

No word yet on global availability or pricing. iQOO tends to keep its most aggressive hardware in China, which is a shame because this tablet addresses one of the biggest complaints about gaming tablets: they're all too big. If you've been waiting for a flagship Android tablet that doesn't require two hands and a backpack, the Pad Ultra might be the first real option. Whether it stays exclusive to China or makes its way west is the only question that matters now.

item.title: JBL Cove Tries to Make Multi-Room Audio Simple. We've Heard That Before.
item.description:
JBL just launched Cove, a whole-home Wi-Fi audio system designed to make multi-room listening simple. The emphasis on simple is doing a lot of work in that sentence, because anyone who's wrestled with Sonos grouping bugs or watched a Google Home speaker drop offline mid-song knows that multi-room audio is rarely simple in practice.

The new range includes three wireless speakers that can operate solo, as stereo pairs, or networked together across your home. Everything runs through the JBL One app, which handles room-by-room playback without forcing you to constantly regroup speakers or restart the system. At least, that's the promise. Multi-room audio lives or dies on app stability and network handoffs, and JBL's track record with software hasn't exactly been flawless.

What makes Cove interesting is the Dolby Atmos support on select models. Most whole-home systems prioritize convenience over sound quality, treating speakers like interchangeable boxes that pump music into kitchens and bathrooms. If JBL actually delivers spatial audio in a multi-room context without requiring a receiver or soundbar, that would be a meaningful shift. The question is whether Atmos makes sense for background listening, or if it's just a spec sheet talking point.

The elephant in the room is Sonos. JBL is entering a market dominated by a company that spent two decades refining this exact product category, then nearly destroyed customer trust with a botched app redesign. That gives newcomers an opening, but also shows how hard it is to get multi-room audio right. Sonos has years of Wi-Fi mesh optimization and codec licensing deals. JBL has brand recognition in Bluetooth speakers and headphones, but whole-home Wi-Fi is a different game.

Cove's success will hinge on execution details JBL hasn't shared yet. How much do the speakers cost? What streaming services are natively supported? Can you mix Cove speakers with existing JBL products, or is this a walled garden? And most importantly, does the JBL One app actually work when you have five speakers running in different rooms?

Multi-room audio is one of those categories where the idea is always better than the reality. JBL has the audio engineering chops and the brand recognition. Whether they have the software discipline to pull this off is another question entirely.

item.title: John Ternus Just Became Apple's CEO. The Hardware Guy Is In Charge.
item.description:
Apple has a new CEO, and for the first time in over a decade, it's not the supply chain guy calling the shots.

John Ternus officially took over as Apple's chief executive on September 1, 2026, replacing Tim Cook, who moved into an executive chairman role. The transition happened quietly, just days before Apple's biggest product launch of the year—the September 9 event that introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo foldable, Apple Watch Series 12, and AirPods 5.

Ternus isn't a household name, but he's been Apple's senior vice president of hardware engineering since 2021, overseeing the teams that build iPhones, Macs, and the entire M-series chip transition. Before that, he led Mac engineering and played a key role in developing the company's custom silicon strategy. In other words, this is the guy who actually makes the products, not just the guy who gets them built on time and under budget.

That's a meaningful shift. Cook, who ran Apple for 13 years after Steve Jobs, came from operations. His superpower was making Apple the most efficient manufacturing machine in consumer tech. Ternus, by contrast, is a product person. He's an engineer who spent decades in the details of thermal design, chip architecture, and industrial engineering. He knows why the hinge on a foldable iPhone matters, not just how many units shipped in Q3.

The timing is telling. Apple is in the middle of its biggest hardware reinvention in years. The iPhone just went foldable. Macs are getting touchscreens for the first time. Siri is being rebuilt from scratch with on-device AI. These aren't iterative spec bumps—they're bets that require deep product judgment, not just operational excellence.

And Ternus is taking over at a moment when competitors like Google and Samsung are moving faster on AI integration and form-factor experimentation. Apple needs someone who can make hard calls on what ships and what doesn't, not just someone who can optimize the supply chain.

The executive chairman role for Cook isn't ceremonial—he'll still oversee board relations and major partnerships—but the day-to-day product decisions now sit with someone who's been in the room where those products were designed. That could mean faster iteration, weirder experiments, or just a different kind of Apple.

Either way, the hardware guy is in charge now. And the first products on his watch just shipped.

item.title: Meta's Muse Charm Has No Price and No Ship Date. That's the Story.
item.description:
Meta announced a pocket AI device at Connect on Wednesday, and the most interesting details are the ones Mark Zuckerberg didn't provide. The Muse Charm is a keychain-sized gadget built to carry Meta's Muse AI agent with you, letting you talk to it without unlocking your phone. It has a 2-inch OLED touchscreen, built-in 5G, microphones, speakers, cameras on both sides, and a fingerprint sensor. Meta says it'll ship in December.

Here's what Meta didn't say: how much it costs. Or whether the hardware design is actually final. Zuckerberg told the audience his team still needs to "finalize laying out the components." That's an unusual thing to admit onstage about a product supposedly shipping in three months, and it suggests Meta accelerated the timeline to beat competitors to market rather than because the Charm was ready.

The device shows a cartoon avatar called Jolly on its screen, meant to be the visible face of Muse. You can speak to it, show it things with the cameras, and interact without pulling out a phone. The pitch is familiar because we've heard it twice before. Humane's AI Pin cost $699 plus a subscription and promised to replace your phone; HP bought the company's assets in early 2025 and shut the devices down. Rabbit's R1 launched at $199 in 2024 and got savaged in reviews. Meta itself acquired Limitless in December 2025, a company that sold a $99 pendant for recording conversations, then stopped selling it.

What Meta has that those companies didn't is an AI agent people already know and an ecosystem of hardware to plug it into. Muse will work across Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses, the new audio-only glasses launching in October for $349, and eventually the $1,299 VR Glasses shipping next spring. The Charm is meant to be the option when you're not wearing any of those, a standalone device that lives on your keychain.

The question isn't whether Meta can build this thing. It's whether anyone actually wants to clip a microphone-equipped AI assistant to their keys and talk to it in public. Smartphones work because they're private, discreet, and multipurpose. A pendant that only does one thing, that requires you to speak aloud to use it, that broadcasts to everyone around you that you're talking to an AI, faces a much higher bar. Humane and Rabbit couldn't clear it. Meta thinks software people already use will make the difference.

We'll find out in December. Assuming the components fit.

item.title: Clicks Communicator Just Got Better Specs. And a Battery Downgrade.
item.description:
Clicks updated the Communicator on September 18 with a spec sheet that reads like a lesson in compromise. The physical keyboard phone now packs 12GB of RAM instead of 8GB, and the battery bumped from 4,000 mAh to 4,350 mAh. Good news, right?

Not quite. That battery upgrade comes with an asterisk the size of a safety warning: Clicks ditched its silicon-carbon battery chemistry entirely and switched back to conventional lithium-ion. The reason? The silicon-carbon cells were failing third-party battery tests at rates high enough to spook the company into retreat.

Silicon-carbon batteries promise higher energy density and faster charging than lithium-ion, which is why Clicks bet on them in the first place. But the technology is still young, and turns out those promises don't mean much if the cells can't pass basic reliability testing. The switch to lithium-ion is the safe move, but it also means the Communicator is now running the same battery tech as nearly every other phone on the market.

There's one more wrinkle in the battery story: an earlier announcement pegged capacity at 4,450 mAh, but the final spec landed at 4,350 mAh. No explanation was given for the 100 mAh haircut, but it's a reminder that even when a company upgrades, you still need to read the footnotes.

The RAM bump to 12GB is straightforward good news, especially for a device trying to balance Android multitasking with a physical keyboard workflow. More headroom for keeping apps in memory matters when you're constantly switching between messaging, email, and whatever else justifies carrying a phone with actual keys in 2026.

Clicks also showed off a demo of its Signal Light feature, which is still in development, and announced an on-device speech-to-text model. That last bit is worth watching. On-device processing means transcription happens without round-tripping to the cloud, which is faster, more private, and actually useful when your keyboard phone loses signal in a basement.

The Communicator remains a niche product, but this update shows Clicks is at least paying attention to the details. The company just learned the hard way that bleeding-edge battery tech isn't worth the risk if it can't clear the safety bar. Lithium-ion might be boring, but boring batteries don't recall themselves.

item.title: Google's Pixel 11 Can Now Make Phone Calls For You With Gemini
item.description:
Google is pushing the boundaries of AI-powered smartphone features in a way that feels both impressive and deeply uncomfortable. The company just announced that select Gemini Advanced subscribers who own a Pixel 11 will soon be able to hand off their phone calls to Google's AI chatbot.

The feature does exactly what it sounds like: when you need to make a call — say, to reschedule a dentist appointment or check restaurant hours — Gemini can dial, navigate phone trees, speak to whoever picks up, and relay the information back to you. It's an extension of the call screening features Google has been building for years, but this time the AI isn't just listening. It's talking.

From a pure convenience standpoint, the appeal is obvious. Phone calls remain one of the last bastions of genuine friction in daily life, especially for administrative tasks nobody wants to do. Letting AI handle the hold music and repetitive questions sounds great.

But there's something unsettling about outsourcing human conversation to a chatbot without the person on the other end necessarily knowing they're not talking to you. Google hasn't detailed how transparent the feature will be during calls, which matters a lot. Will businesses know they're speaking to an AI? Will your dentist's receptionist realize she's rescheduling with software?

The Pixel 11 exclusivity also highlights an emerging pattern: Google is using its Gemini subscription tier and its own hardware to gate its most ambitious AI experiments. That makes sense from a controlled rollout perspective, but it does mean you'll need both the phone and the $20-per-month Gemini Advanced plan to even try this.

It's not clear yet when the feature will actually roll out beyond the initial test group. Google has been steadily adding AI call capabilities to Pixel phones over the past few years — first with screening, then with hold-for-me, and now full conversation delegation. Each step inches closer to a world where your phone is less a communication device and more a personal assistant that occasionally impersonates you.

Whether that's the future we want is a different question than whether it's the future we're getting.

item.title: Meta Just Killed the Camera. Its New Ray-Bans Are Audio Only.
item.description:
Meta just did something it rarely does: it made a gadget with fewer features. The [Ray-Ban Meta Audio](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ray-Ban+Meta+Audio&tag=techtreck02-20), announced at Connect 2026 and shipping October 13, strips out the camera entirely. No photos, no video, no 12-megapixel sensor recording everything you see. Just audio, AI, and $349.

It's the first time Meta has shipped smart glasses without a camera since the Ray-Ban partnership began in 2021. The company is betting there's a market for people who want AI assistance and decent audio without the privacy baggage that comes with a lens pointed at the world. Given how much heat Meta has taken over recording without consent, the bet makes sense.

The glasses come in Clubmaster and Burbank frame styles with 23 frame and lens combinations, weigh 43 grams, and promise 12 hours of battery life. They use open-ear speakers, support prescriptions, and include adjustable temple tips and interchangeable nose pads. Meta AI is baked in, accessible through voice commands, though you won't be asking it to identify objects or translate signs since there's no camera to feed it visual data.

What you lose is obvious: no quick photo capture, no hands-free video recording, no visual context for the AI. What you gain is less obvious but potentially more important for some buyers: you can wear these in places where cameras raise eyebrows or violate policy. Gyms, locker rooms, secure workplaces, or just around people who don't want to be recorded.

Meta also announced the third-generation Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses at the same event, keeping the 12-megapixel camera but adding new Aviator and Zena frames, six microphones instead of five, and battery life up to nine hours. Those start at $449, available now. There's even a limited-edition Aviator celebrating the frame's 90th anniversary.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio feels less like a stripped-down version and more like Meta acknowledging that not everyone wants a face computer that captures everything. Some people just want better audio and an AI assistant without the camera constantly explaining itself. At $100 less than the camera-equipped model, it's a clear value proposition for anyone who never planned to use the lens anyway.

Whether the market actually wants camera-free smart glasses is another question. Meta's previous models sold well specifically because of the camera convenience during travel, sports, and everyday moments. But if you've been holding out on smart glasses purely because of privacy concerns, Meta just removed your excuse.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro Is Now in Stores. Here's What Actually Changed.
item.description:
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max hit stores five days ago, and if you're wondering whether this year's Pro phones are worth the upgrade, the answer hinges almost entirely on how much you care about the camera.

Apple kept the September 9 event focused on its foldable iPhone Duo experiment, but the actual workhorses of this year's lineup are the two Pro models that launched September 18. Both phones ship with the new A20 Pro chip, which is exactly as fast as you'd expect and exactly as irrelevant to most people's daily usage as every iPhone chip for the past three years. The real story is what Apple did to the cameras and the battery.

The iPhone 18 Pro gets what Apple is calling major camera upgrades, though the company was characteristically vague about sensor sizes and processing tweaks during the keynote. What we do know: the Dynamic Island is smaller, which matters more than it should because that floating pill still interrupts video playback in annoying ways. Apple also introduced new colors, because of course they did.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is where things get interesting. Apple claims this is the most battery-efficient iPhone ever built, pairing a larger battery with the same A20 Pro chip to squeeze out measurably longer screen-on time. If you've been waiting for an iPhone that can comfortably survive a full day of heavy use without anxiety, this might finally be it.

Both models opened for pre-order on September 12, which means early adopters have had their phones for less than a week. The usual caveats apply: we're still in the honeymoon period where every new iPhone feels impossibly fast and every screen looks impossibly bright. Real-world battery numbers won't settle in for another couple of weeks.

What's more notable is what Apple didn't do. The base iPhone 18 won't arrive until early 2027, leaving a massive gap in the lineup and forcing anyone who wants a new iPhone this fall to pay Pro prices. It's the smallest flagship iPhone lineup in years and the most expensive, which feels like Apple testing just how much margin the market will tolerate.

If you're upgrading from an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, nothing here is essential. If you're still holding an iPhone 13 or earlier and you've been waiting for the right moment, the 18 Pro Max's battery life might be enough to tip the scales. Just know that you're paying more for less choice than you would have two years ago, and Apple is betting you won't care.

item.title: Qualcomm's New Snapdragon Chip Has Two Names and a 5GHz Problem
item.description:
Qualcomm just announced not one but two flagship processors for next-generation Android phones, and the naming situation has officially gotten out of hand. Say hello to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Yes, Extreme is now an official tier, sitting above Elite, which was already meant to signal premium. It's confusing, it's excessive, and somehow it's real.

But the chips themselves are legitimately impressive. Both are built on a 2nm process and feature Qualcomm's Oryon CPU with two Prime cores running at 5GHz and six Performance cores at 4GHz. That makes these the first smartphone processors to break the 5GHz barrier, beating the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy's 4.74GHz ceiling. The standard Elite Gen 6 delivers a 10% CPU performance bump and 37% better power efficiency compared to last year's Gen 5, while the Extreme variant pushes that to a 13% CPU improvement.

The real differentiator is the Extreme's video capabilities. It supports 8K video recording at 60fps and 4K slow motion at 240fps, a massive leap for smartphone videography. The Extreme also gets Matrix Cores baked into the Adreno GPU, enabling what Qualcomm calls Adreno Neural Fusion for more advanced upscaling and frame generation with 40% power savings. The GPU performance gains are substantial: 35% for the standard Gen 6, 44% for the Extreme.

Qualcomm also crammed in a new Flex Cache architecture that lets cores dynamically share a 16MB L2 cache pool, plus a beefed-up Hexagon NPU that can run AI models with over 30 billion parameters directly on-device. The Extreme variant gets 50% more shared memory for the NPU, allowing it to handle even larger models without constantly hitting external memory.

Phones powered by these chips are coming fast. Motorola already announced the Signature 27 with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, and Qualcomm says devices from HONOR, iQOO, OnePlus, OPPO, REDMI, RedMagic, vivo, and Xiaomi will arrive before the end of 2026. Expect the Galaxy S27 family to follow early next year.

The performance story is strong. The name? Still ridiculous.

item.title: Xiaomi Just Built Its Own M5 Competitor. It Costs $715.
item.description:
Xiaomi just launched the Pad 9 Pro Max in China, and it's the company's most audacious tablet move yet: the first device powered entirely by its own silicon, the Xring O3 chip. At 4,799 yuan (about $715), it's positioned as a direct challenge to Apple's iPad Pro 13 with M5, which starts at $1,199. The price gap alone is startling, but the real question is whether Xiaomi's homegrown processor can actually deliver.

The Xring O3 is a 10-core, 3nm chip built exclusively from high-performance cores—two clocked at 4.35GHz, four at 3.68GHz, and four at 3.15GHz—paired with a 16-core Mali-G2-Ultra GPU. Xiaomi claims the chip achieves CPU and GPU performance approaching Apple's M5, with AnTuTu scores exceeding 5.61 million points. That's a bold claim, especially given that Geekbench multi-core results hover around 14,000 points, which is strong but not quite desktop-chip territory. Independent testing will tell the real story, but on paper, this is Xiaomi's most serious attempt yet to compete with Apple and Qualcomm on its own terms.

The hardware backing that chip is impressive. The Pad 9 Pro Max features a 13.3-inch 3.4K display with a 3:2 aspect ratio, 144Hz refresh rate, and 1,000 nits peak brightness. It's absurdly thin at 5.67mm and weighs just 645 grams despite packing a 12,000mAh battery with 120W fast charging. The tablet also includes a clever DP-in feature via USB-C, letting it function as a secondary 3.4K monitor for laptops or gaming consoles. Add Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, eight speakers, and support for up to 16GB of RAM, and you've got a spec sheet that genuinely rivals premium tablets.

The catch? Xiaomi hasn't announced any plans for a US, UK, or broader international launch. That's typical for the company's most experimental hardware, but it's frustrating given how competitive this pricing is. The top-tier 16GB/1TB configuration with an anti-glare matte display costs 7,899 yuan (around $1,176)—still cheaper than the equivalent iPad Pro.

Whether the Xring O3 can truly hang with Apple's M5 in sustained workloads, gaming, and video editing remains to be seen. But Xiaomi is clearly serious about building its own chip ecosystem, and the Pad 9 Pro Max is the first tablet that makes that ambition feel credible. If it ever ships globally, Apple should pay attention.

item.title: DJI Avata 360 Makes 360 Drones Actually Worth Buying
item.description:
360 drones were a novelty until about six months ago. Shoot everything, reframe later — neat idea, terrible execution. The Antigravity A1 changed that calculus somewhat when it launched as the first serious attempt at making 360 aerial footage usable. But at $1,599, it was a tough sell for anyone who wasn't already deep into immersive video.

Then DJI released the Avata 360 in April, and the pricing conversation got a lot more interesting. At $719 for the standalone drone in the US — or $409-$459 in other markets — it undercuts the A1 by more than $500 while delivering specs that actually read better on paper. Dual 1-inch equivalent sensors. 8K/60fps HDR 360° video. 120MP stills. And here's the part that matters: it can also shoot traditional 4K/60fps FPV footage when you flip to single-lens mode.

That versatility is the entire pitch. If you already fly FPV and want one drone that handles both styles, the Avata 360 is the first time that's been a realistic option. The A1 is lighter at sub-250 grams, which matters in some regulatory environments, but the Avata 360's 455-gram weight gets you 23 minutes of flight time and compatibility with DJI's existing goggles and controllers. If you own a DJI RC 2 or Goggles N3, you're not paying twice for redundant gear.

TechRadar called it their new favorite 360 drone a few weeks ago, and the reasoning tracks. The A1 shoots 8K/30fps; the Avata 360 does 8K/60. The A1 with its high-capacity battery gets 39 minutes of flight time, but that tips it over the 250-gram threshold that made it appealing in the first place. And while the A1 requires buying into an entirely new ecosystem, the Avata 360 slots into a platform millions of people already use.

There are trade-offs. The Avata 360 isn't officially sold through DJI's US site due to regulatory uncertainty, though it's widely available through Amazon and B&H Photo and was grandfathered in under FCC rules before last year's ban discussions. And 23 minutes of flight time means you'll want extra batteries if you're shooting anything longer than quick reels.

But this is the first time 360 drones feel like a category that might actually matter. Not because the tech got radically better — it didn't — but because someone finally priced it like a tool instead of a luxury experiment. At $719, the Avata 360 is expensive enough to feel serious and cheap enough that creators who've been curious about 360 video can justify the jump. That's the gap DJI needed to hit, and they nailed it.

item.title: PS5 Pro Just Got Smarter About Graphics. You Don't Have to Do Anything.
item.description:
Sony just pushed out PS5 system software version 26.06-14.00.00 on September 16, and buried in the patch notes is a change that matters more than most firmware updates: Enhanced PSSR Image Quality now turns itself on automatically for every PS5 Pro owner. No menu hunting, no per-game toggle. Update your console and you're done.

PSSR stands for PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, Sony's AI-driven upscaling tech that's one of the main reasons to buy a PS5 Pro in the first place. The enhanced version debuted back in March 2026 as an optional setting tucked away in the Video Output menu. It improved on the original PSSR implementation, delivering sharper image quality in supported games. But you had to know it existed and manually flip the switch.

Not anymore. The September update makes Enhanced PSSR the console's default behavior. Any game that already supported the original PSSR automatically inherits the upgraded upscaling pipeline, whether or not the developer has explicitly certified it for the new version. According to ComputerBase's tracking, that covers more than 100 games—well beyond Sony's official list of PSSR 2.0-certified titles.

It sounds like a small tweak. It's not. Sony is effectively declaring that AI upscaling isn't an optional graphics setting anymore—it's platform infrastructure. By switching Enhanced PSSR on by default instead of leaving it opt-in, Sony is signaling confidence that the upgrade is a net improvement across the board, not a feature with enough edge cases to warrant a cautious rollout.

The update also brings a few quality-of-life additions for all PS5 owners, including a voice chat speaker indicator that shows who's talking during party chat, and a new Community Activity widget in the Welcome Hub that surfaces trending games. There's also a somewhat niche addition: a setting to disable Bluetooth entirely, intended for esports venues that need tighter controller connection management. Flipping that switch also turns off HDMI Device Link and rest mode, so it's not something most people should touch.

If you've set your PS5 to auto-update, version 26.06-14.00.00 is probably already installed. If not, you can grab it manually through the system settings. Pro owners who preferred the old PSSR behavior can still toggle Enhanced PSSR off by navigating to Settings > Screen and Video > Video Output > Enhance PSSR Image Quality, but Sony is clearly betting most people won't bother.

Two years after the PS5 Pro launched, this is the kind of update that justifies the existence of mid-generation refreshes. The hardware shipped with the capability. Now Sony is finally making sure every owner actually uses it.

item.title: Xbox and IKEA Built Furniture From Controller CAD Files. It Ships Next Week.
item.description:
IKEA and Xbox just confirmed something genuinely weird: a nine-piece furniture collection launching October 1 that's built directly from the engineering files of an actual Xbox controller. Not inspired by. Built from the same CAD data that defines the thumbsticks and D-pad you've been mashing for 25 years.

The YXSTABY collection includes a thumbstick stool that rocks when you sit on it, a D-pad cushion, a lounge chair with a mesh controller holder built into the side, and a mirrored display case designed specifically for showing off controllers and collectibles. Prices run from $18 for the D-pad platter to $180 for the side table on casters. Buy all nine pieces and you're out about $575.

What separates this from the usual gamer furniture playbook is restraint. IKEA's 2021 ASUS ROG collaboration leaned hard into black geometric aggression. This one barely registers as gaming furniture at all unless you've spent enough time with an Xbox controller to recognize the exact curve of a thumbstick translated into a 35-pound stool. The palette is neutral grays and whites with occasional flashes of Xbox green. The shapes are subtle enough that a non-gamer walking into your living room would probably just think you have eclectic taste.

That's the point, apparently. Xbox's Carl Ledbetter said the team designed every piece to sit naturally alongside furniture people already own, not dominate a dedicated gaming cave. IKEA's Philip Dilé framed it as solving the problem of gaming setups that need to work in shared spaces where not everyone cares about your hobby.

The thumbstick stool is the obvious conversation piece here. It tilts slightly when you sit on it, mimicking the movement of an actual analog stick, and comes in black or bright green for $50. The lounge chair at $128 includes a dedicated pouch that holds a controller at arm's reach without looking like a tactical gear attachment. The TV stand on casters holds two monitors, clips for headphones and controllers, and costs $155.

The collection goes on sale in US stores October 1 and online November 30. UK and Canadian launch is October 1 across the board. IKEA says availability is while stocks last, which is a polite way of saying this might sell out fast if the internet decides thumbstick stools are the new Billy bookcase.

It's a strange collaboration that somehow makes sense. Xbox gets to mark its 25th anniversary with something more tangible than a limited-edition controller shell. IKEA gets to prove it can do gaming furniture that doesn't scream "gaming furniture." And you get to explain to guests why you're sitting on a giant green joystick.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 Quietly Became the Most Important Watch Release
item.description:
Apple's September event was supposed to be all about the foldable iPhone Duo and the Ultra 4's flashy new features. But buried in the middle of that presentation was something more interesting: the Apple Watch Series 12, which might be the most thoughtful product Apple shipped this year.

The Series 12 doesn't reinvent the smartwatch. It doesn't need to. What it does is refine the formula in ways that actually matter for the millions of people who wear an Apple Watch every day, not just the weekend warriors who need multi-day battery life and depth gauges.

Apple equipped the Series 12 with a more powerful chip, presumably the S12, which enables better health tracking and faster performance. More importantly, it brings the same health features that have historically been reserved for the Ultra line, making advanced wellness monitoring accessible at a lower price point. Pre-orders opened on September 9, the same day as the event, with immediate availability for most models.

The timing here is smart. Apple is clearly trying to consolidate its wearable lineup and push more sophisticated health features down the stack. That's good news for consumers who don't need the rugged titanium build and extreme sports features of the Ultra but still want serious health monitoring.

What sets the Series 12 apart from previous standard models is its positioning. This isn't just an incremental spec bump. It's Apple acknowledging that the average Apple Watch customer has gotten more sophisticated about health tracking and expects more from their device. The gap between the standard Series model and the Ultra has been too wide for too long.

The price point wasn't explicitly mentioned in what I found, but historically the Series models have started around $399. If Apple maintains that pricing while adding features that previously required an $800 Ultra purchase, that's a significant value shift.

The real question is whether this cannibalizes Ultra 4 sales or simply expands the market. My guess is the latter. The people buying the Ultra aren't doing it just for health features; they're buying the design language, the titanium, the bigger battery, and the bragging rights. The Series 12 serves everyone else who wants a very good smartwatch without the premium price tag.

Apple's wearable strategy has always been about expanding the tent, and the Series 12 feels like the next logical step. It's not the flashiest thing Apple announced this fall, but it might be the one that matters most.

item.title: Dyson Built a $500 Electric Toothbrush With a Camera Inside
item.description:
Dyson, a company that's made its name selling premium vacuums and bladeless fans, has decided the next frontier is your mouth. The Dyson CameraJet is an electric toothbrush that arrives at Best Buy this September with a feature that sounds either brilliant or dystopian depending on your tolerance for surveillance: a built-in camera that livestreams the inside of your mouth.

According to TechRadar, the CameraJet takes some getting used to—the water spray mechanism feels foreign at first—but becomes comfortable after a learning curve. That spray system is paired with USB-C charging that delivers up to eight hours of battery life, though your mileage will vary across the three intensity settings.

The real draw here is the MyDyson app, which doesn't just show you a livestream of your dental work in real time. It also delivers guided brushing sessions designed to ensure you're hitting every surface properly. It's the sort of over-engineered approach Dyson has become known for, and whether you find it helpful or excessive probably depends on how much you trust yourself to brush correctly without AI assistance.

The price hasn't been officially confirmed in all markets, but NBC Select flagged it as part of September's notable product launches alongside the usual Apple hardware. This positions it as a premium play in a category that's increasingly crowded with smart features—from Oral-B's pressure sensors to Philips Sonicare's app coaching.

What's interesting here isn't just that Dyson made a toothbrush. It's that they made a toothbrush with a camera, which suggests the company sees an opening in health-adjacent gadgets where its engineering-first reputation can command a premium. Whether people will pay Dyson prices for dental care is another question entirely, but it's hard to ignore a product this specific and this strange.

The CameraJet is available now at Best Buy and through Dyson's website. If you've ever wondered what your molars look like in 1080p, this is your moment.

item.title: Mac Studio with M5 Chips Ships Tomorrow. Apple Buried the Lede.
item.description:
Tomorrow, September 22, Apple will ship the new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra processors. If that launch date sounds familiar, it's because it's the same day the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max hit stores. Apple announced the Mac Studio last month with barely a whisper, and now it's arriving in one of the busiest product launches the company has had in years.

The new Mac Studio starts at $2,499 and comes configured with either the M5 Max or M5 Ultra chip. For anyone keeping count, that's Apple's desktop workstation slotting into a launch window that also includes two flagship iPhones, a foldable iPhone Ultra that shipped last week, two new Apple Watch models, AirPods 5, and potentially a handful of smart home products.

It's a strange bit of timing. The Mac Studio is a serious machine aimed at video editors, developers, and creative professionals who need desktop-class power in a compact form factor. Those buyers don't typically overlap with the iPhone upgrade crowd, and burying a workstation launch in the middle of Apple's annual phone frenzy feels like a missed opportunity to let the hardware breathe.

The M5 Max and M5 Ultra represent meaningful performance upgrades over the M2-generation chips in the previous Mac Studio, which hasn't been refreshed since early 2023. The new silicon should deliver substantial gains in rendering, compiling, and anything that leans hard on GPU compute. But the conversation around this machine has been drowned out by the iPhone spectacle and the iPhone Ultra's creaseless foldable display.

Apple clearly wanted to pack September with as many launches as possible. The company is also shipping the new Mac mini on the same day, creating a double desktop launch that would normally warrant its own event or at least a focused PR push. Instead, both machines are getting lost in the noise.

For anyone in the market for a Mac Studio, tomorrow is the day. Just don't expect much fanfare when it arrives. Apple's already moved on to the next thing.

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4's Live Rewind Feature Makes Memory Optional
item.description:
Apple's latest flagship smartwatch landed at Best Buy this week with a $799 price tag and one feature that feels both futuristic and vaguely unsettling: Live Rewind. Double-tap the digital crown and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 plays back the last 15 seconds of ambient audio it's been continuously recording. Zoned out during your boss's instructions? Forgot what your partner just asked you to pick up from the store? The watch remembers, even if you don't.

It's the kind of feature that sounds gimmicky until you think about the edge cases where it actually matters. Missing critical information in loud environments, catching details you didn't realize were important in the moment, or simply having a backup when your brain decides to take an unscheduled coffee break. The watch is essentially functioning as a rolling buffer of your acoustic environment, which raises obvious privacy questions Apple will need to address clearly.

The Ultra 4 runs on Apple's new S11 chip, which powers the Live Rewind feature and enables what Apple is calling Siri AI features. Performance is reportedly smoother than the Ultra 3, though Apple hasn't detailed exactly what the AI label means beyond marketing speak. The display carries over from last year's model, which isn't surprising given how bright and sharp the Ultra 3's screen already was.

Battery life gets a meaningful bump, though Apple's official rating wasn't mentioned in early coverage. For a watch that's supposed to handle multi-day adventures, every extra hour counts, and the Ultra line has historically overpromised and underdelivered on longevity compared to dedicated outdoor watches from Garmin or Suunto.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 launched alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models and other products at Apple's September 2026 event, dubbed Surprise and Shine. At $799, it sits exactly where the Ultra 3 did at launch, which makes sense. The Live Rewind feature alone gives Apple something concrete to market beyond incremental speed bumps.

Whether that feature becomes genuinely useful or just another checkbox on the spec sheet depends entirely on how well Apple handles the privacy implications and how reliably it works in real-world chaos. But as a statement of where wearables are headed, continuous ambient recording with instant playback is either brilliant or deeply creepy. Probably both.

item.title: HTC Vive Eagle Arrives to Challenge Ray-Ban Meta at $499
item.description:
HTC spent a year keeping its Vive Eagle smart glasses locked to Taiwan. Now they're finally shipping across North America, Europe, the UK, and Australia, arriving just as the smart glasses category starts feeling less like a novelty and more like an actual product segment people buy.

The pitch is straightforward: lightweight AI eyewear that doesn't try to cram a display into your face. At 49 grams with lenses, the Vive Eagle goes head-to-head with Meta's Ray-Ban collaboration, offering a 12MP ultra-wide camera for stabilized 3K video, open-ear directional speakers, and your choice of Google Gemini or ChatGPT as your voice-activated assistant. The dual AI option is the notable differentiator here—Meta locks you into its own ecosystem, while HTC lets you pick your poison.

Pricing starts at $499 for standard or sun lenses, jumping to $599 if you want photochromic auto-darkening glass. That's a $200 premium over the entry-level Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses, which makes the value proposition trickier. HTC partnered with Zeiss for the optics and supports prescription inserts, so at least the glasses-as-glasses part is taken seriously. You get two frame styles, square or round, across multiple colorways including glossy coffee and navy.

The spec sheet reads competently: Snapdragon AR Gen 1 chip, 4GB RAM, 32GB storage, IP54 rating, and a 235mAh battery good for about 4.5 hours of music playback or 36 hours on standby. HTC ditched the charging case in favor of a magnetic pogo pin cable that snaps on while you're still wearing them, hitting 50 percent in ten minutes. There's also an optional $49 Power Boost accessory that clips onto the frame and adds 80 percent more juice.

AI features include live translation across 13 languages, hands-free note-taking, and voice-triggered photo capture. A visible LED lights up when the camera records, and HTC promises local storage with encryption for photos and videos, clearly trying to sidestep the privacy concerns that have dogged Meta's glasses.

The bigger question is whether HTC can carve out meaningful space against an incumbent that's already sold enough units to make smart glasses feel credible. The dual AI assistant angle is clever, and the Zeiss partnership adds optical credibility. But asking consumers to pay double for those extras assumes people care enough about AI flexibility to spend the premium. That's a harder sell than HTC probably wants to admit.

US buyers can order now with immediate shipping. European and UK customers wait until September 21. Every purchase includes a two-year subscription to Vive AI Plus, which presumably unlocks additional features HTC will detail later. Whether that sweetens the deal enough to justify the price remains to be seen.

item.title: Razer Just Released Xbox-Branded Versions of Its Best Gaming Gear
item.description:
Razer's made Xbox-branded versions of three of its core gaming peripherals, and they're shipping now. You get the Hammerhead V3 X HyperSpeed wireless earbuds, the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K gaming mouse, and the BlackWidow V4 75% mechanical keyboard—all dressed in Xbox green and black livery, each bundled with one month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate.

It's a smart move on both sides. Razer gets to tap into Xbox's massive console ecosystem, while Microsoft strengthens its pitch that Game Pass isn't just for console players. These are PC peripherals first, which reinforces the message that Game Pass Ultimate works across platforms.

The Basilisk V3 Pro 35K is the headliner here. The "35K" refers to its 35,000 DPI optical sensor, which is borderline absurd for actual gaming but useful for productivity on high-res displays. More importantly, it's one of Razer's best wireless mice, with low latency, customizable buttons, and solid battery life. Slapping Xbox branding on it makes it an easier sell to someone already invested in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The BlackWidow V4 75% is Razer's compact mechanical keyboard—75% layout means you keep the arrow keys and a few nav keys while ditching the numpad. It's a format that's become hugely popular with gamers who want tactile switches but don't have infinite desk space. The Xbox edition likely uses the same Green or Yellow switches Razer's known for, which are fine if not exceptional in the broader mechanical keyboard market.

Then there are the Hammerhead V3 X HyperSpeed earbuds, which are Razer's wireless gaming buds with low-latency connectivity via USB-C dongle. They're not AirPods competitors—they're purpose-built for gaming with emphasis on spatial audio and minimal lag, though the sound quality for music tends to be just okay.

The one-month Game Pass Ultimate sweetener is a nice touch, even if it's mostly a trial designed to get you hooked on the subscription. For someone buying into the Xbox ecosystem for the first time, it's value-add. For existing subscribers, it's a mild bonus.

What Razer hasn't done is create genuinely new products here. These are cosmetic variants of existing hardware with bundled software. That's not necessarily a problem—the underlying gear is solid—but don't expect any exclusive features or performance tweaks. You're paying for the green logo and the Game Pass trial, nothing more.

Still, if you're already in the market for any of these three categories and you like the Xbox aesthetic, these aren't bad choices. Just know you're buying established Razer hardware with a new coat of paint.

item.title: Apple's iPhone Duo Won't Ship Until October Despite This Week's Event
item.description:
Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone at its September 9 event this week, but if you were planning to get your hands on one immediately, you're out of luck. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the device—officially called the iPhone Duo—will go on sale as early as October, not alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models that were announced at the same event.

The staggered launch is notable because Apple typically ships flagship products within a week or two of announcement. The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are already available for pre-order with standard September ship dates, while the Duo gets pushed to next month at minimum. That "as early as October" phrasing suggests even that timeline isn't locked in.

It's a familiar playbook. Apple did something similar with the iPhone X back in 2017, announcing it alongside the iPhone 8 but delaying shipments by several weeks. The difference here is that foldables are notoriously difficult to manufacture at scale, and Apple is entering a market where Samsung, Motorola, and others have been iterating for years. A delay to get the hinge mechanism and display durability right makes sense, even if it's frustrating for early adopters.

The iPhone Duo joins a crowded September lineup that includes the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. The Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips also started shipping on September 22 with prices beginning at $2,499, though the 512GB unified memory configuration won't arrive until late October.

For context, Apple isn't releasing a standard iPhone 18 this year. The company is focusing its September lineup exclusively on premium models, leaving the base-tier iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 pushed to early 2027. That makes the Duo delay even more conspicuous—Apple's most experimental device of the year is also the one customers will have to wait longest for.

The October ship date means Apple will collect pre-orders and build hype through the end of September without actually delivering hardware. Whether that's a deliberate scarcity play or a genuine production constraint, the message is clear: if you want Apple's first foldable, patience is required.
